en: The Śramaṇa Ji composed this treatise.
This meaning has three brief distinctions. The commentary states:
Above, based on the tenth section of the verses, the analysis of the stages of subduing and severing has already been briefly completed. From here below is the second [section], concerning the cause.
Regarding the section on the meaning of the vehicle, its stages, and its modes of activity, there are three parts:
first, indicating the number of distinctions among the stages and modes of activity; second, listing their names;
and third, providing detailed explanations according to each.
This is the first [point]. The treatise states:
"A single person (pudgala) reaches the stage of being associated with the wisdom of equality."
The commentary states:
This is the enumeration of names.
It clarifies the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of consciousness by means of associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*).
Treatise:
First, it pervades all stages up to the state of the mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Commentary states:
Because these three types differ in their brevity and length, distinct stages are established. Below, there is a detailed explanation in two parts:
first, the individual analysis of the three stages;
second, a further clarification through refutation.
This is the first [type of view] associated with the view of a self and what belongs to a self (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*).
*Pudgala* is the correct term;
it is comprised within the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).
It is not only because of humans;
as has already been explained previously,
this refers to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) without exception.
Because those in the stage of the impure mind of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha learners give rise to this view;
[this applies] from the eighth bhūmi upward, excluding that stage.
They never again give rise to this view of a self and what belongs to a self.
Regarding the phrase "a certain class" [of bodhisattvas], it refers to those bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage who are in a state of contaminated mind.
This refers specifically to Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment from the first to the seventh bhūmi;
and to Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment and those of the two vehicles in training (*śaikṣa*), from their initial generation of the mind through the first two asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
With the exception of those bodhisattvas who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment] from the stage of no-more-learning in the two vehicles,
it is said that they belong to "one class," because such individuals are forever non-existent for them.
Regarding this Bodhisattva and those of the Two Vehicles who are still in training (*śaikṣa*), when they give rise to a mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*),
it is because for those who have given rise [only] to the untainted (*anāsrava*), the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) necessarily does not exist. Thus says the Treatise (*śāstra*).
"That [consciousness] takes the ālayavijñāna as its object and gives rise to the view of a person (pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi).
Commentary:
This consciousness takes the ālayavijñāna as its object and gives rise to the view of a "grasper of aggregates" (pudgala).
This is because prior to the seventh stage, the eighth consciousness has not yet relinquished its designation as the *ālayavijñāna*.
Furthermore, it is not that the seventh consciousness does not coexist with the view of phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*);
rather, the duration of this state of viewing phenomena is long.
The stage of the self of persons is brief;
furthermore, the self of persons is coarse,
whereas the self of dharmas is subtle.
Therefore, it is explained partially.
This constitutes the initial non-existence;
this is precisely the relinquishing of names. Question: [What is] that which can take the person-self as its object?
Regarding the statement that it is only when one possesses outflow-tainted (sāsrava) consciousness prior to the seventh stage that [the seeds] are said to exist:
this means they are abandoned upon entering the state of outflow-free (anāsrava) consciousness;
the same applies to what follows.
Regarding the relinquishing of this association:

why is it that the eighth [ground] relinquishes the name "ālayavijñāna," rather than stating that it is relinquished when the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) arises prior to the seventh ground? Answer: The eighth ground refers to permanent relinquishment.
This is because, by nature, one has not yet been able to abandon attachment to others.
Seventh, it is based on temporary relinquishment,
because the defiled entity is absent for a short duration.
There is no contradiction.
It cannot be said that they mutually relinquish [the afflictions],
because those in training (śaikṣa) of the two vehicles have not yet attained what is called "relinquishment."
If it were granted that [the defiled manas] is temporarily abandoned,
then the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas in the stage of training (śaikṣa), when entering an uncontaminated mind, would also have to be said to abandon it,
because the defiled manas is incompatible with the uncontaminated.
Treatise:
Next, it pervades all states up to the stage where [the object] is no longer manifest before one.
Commentary: [As follows].
This is the second [type of] view associated with the Dharma (*dharmadarśana-saṃprayukta*).
If this [second stage] exists in the first stage, it necessarily possesses this [second] stage;
however, when this [second] stage exists, it does not necessarily possess the first.
This state is extensive;
it includes all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
as well as the entire bodies of all followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), whether they be those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
All bodhisattvas include both those who have attained sudden enlightenment and those bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment who are still in training or have completed their training.

Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it refers to the state in which the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and its fruit are not manifest. Regarding "the knowledge of the emptiness of phenomena" (*dharmasunyatājñāna*):
this refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) when entering the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena. As for "its fruit": [it refers to the subsequent attainment].
This is precisely the fruit of this right knowledge;
namely, the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) regarding the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā),
as well as the state of entering meditative absorption (nirodha-samāpatti) by relying on that subsequently attained wisdom regarding the emptiness of phenomena.
Because it is produced by non-conceptual wisdom,
it is called the "fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.
At this time, the seventh consciousness necessarily gives rise to the wisdom of equality.
The sixth dharma is the subtle emptiness of mind.
The seventh dharma is the attachment that obstructs the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatājñāna*).
Because the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena arises, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is produced.
The same applies to the outflowing results (*niṣyanda*),
because their essential nature and category are identical.
However, regarding what is said here:
Briefly stated, these are: the non-conceptual wisdom of the emptiness of persons,
the subsequently attained wisdom following the realization of the emptiness of persons,
and the meditative absorption of cessation induced by this emptiness of persons.
At this stage, although the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*) has been extinguished,
the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still persists; thus,
the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) remains coarse.
The subtle grasping at phenomena does not obstruct that wisdom;
only the seventh person’s grasping at a self can obstruct it.
Therefore, upon entering the stage of observing persons, the grasping at a self no longer functions.
At the stage of the Tathāgata-bhūmi, this consciousness is untainted (anāsrava);
therefore, it is not mentioned.
[Treatise]
"That [mind] takes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) as its object and gives rise to the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātman-dṛṣṭi*).
Commentary states:
"This mind that clings to phenomena (*dharmanirūpaṇa-citta*) takes the ripening consciousness as its object and gives rise to the view of a self in phenomena."
Since the stage of the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātmadṛṣṭi*) is long-lasting,
the mind of maturation (*vipākacitta*) is likewise;
because the seeing [faculty] and its object correspond, it is said to "take [them] as an object" (*ālambate*).
The mind that clings to non-humans does not take maturation as its object;
because the state of maturation is long-lasting, it is not mentioned in relation to them.
The mind that clings to dharmas does not take the ālayavijñāna as its object.
Because the ālayavijñāna is brief, it is not mentioned here. According to the treatise,
it subsequently pervades all [consciousnesses] until the stage where they manifest before one.
The commentary states:
This refers to the mind associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
The subsequent sections provide a complete exposition of this treatise.
It is the entirety of all Tathāgatas,
because it is free from outflows;
it is the entirety of the path of vision for all Bodhisattvas.
This pertains to both sudden and gradual enlightenment;
for all bodhisattvas must enter the path of seeing (darśanamārga) through the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā).
This is not the meaning of the "three moments" of the true path of seeing.
Furthermore, because all Bodhisattvas, during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and when the fruit is manifest,
give rise to the wisdom of equality regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatājñāna*).
People do not perceive it as such,
as has already been explained above;
however, there is a remote fruit within the fruit.
Regarding the question of how there can be proximate results,
the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
If the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) were the outflow (nisyanda) of the contemplation of dharmas (dharmālambana),
it would itself be the contemplation of dharmas; if that were the case,
from the eighth stage (bhūmi) onward, one would never emerge from untainted contemplation (anāsrava-dhyāna).
At what time does that state constitute the fruit of the contemplation of non-dharma?
This should be explained by means of the "proximate fruit.
As stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, following the contemplation of dharma, the subsequently attained [wisdom] manifests.
Regarding the distant fruit:
it is when the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) manifests following the person’s contemplation (*puruṣa-vicāra*);

or, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onwards, when non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) enters the person’s contemplation of its own accord, there is no impediment to the arising of that fruit or the subsequently attained wisdom following the person’s contemplation. However, in this context, the explanation is based on the first interpretation concerning the proximate fruit.
If one speaks according to the latter meaning, it refers to the result in its entirety. Furthermore, this result may involve cognitive engagement (*ālambana*) or lack cognitive engagement.
That which lacks cognitive engagement is the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); that which involves cognitive engagement can be understood [as the other attainments].
Treatise:
That [wisdom] takes the stainless as its object and gives rise to the wisdom of equality.
Commentary: [As follows].
What kind of dharmas does this third wisdom take as its object?
At the stage of Buddhahood, it takes the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) and so forth as its object;
that is to say, because it takes the pure eighth consciousness, all conditioned phenomena, and *tathatā* (suchness) as its objects, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used.
The Bodhisattva’s stage of seeing and cultivation takes both the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) as its objects. Question:
If it is admitted that the Bodhisattva also takes suchness as an object, then within the single mind of the seventh consciousness—
The error of [the seventh consciousness] taking both the true and the conventional, the outflowing and the non-outflowing, as its two objects. Answer:
If it is within the Path of True Seeing (*darśanamārga*), or when it is the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, this seventh consciousness—
It exclusively takes suchness as its object and does not take the eighth [consciousness] as its object,
because it is a contemplation of principle alone.
This is its characteristic as the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, within the path of cultivation, the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) of the category of the wisdom of equality (samatā-jñāna) either takes only the eighth consciousness as its object,
or it also takes that which resembles suchness (tathatā) as its object.
In fact, it is only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) that serve as objects;
they universally take both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena as their objective domain because they are specifically induced by the sixth consciousness.
Thus, the present general statement says they "take maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth as objects."
Because they are equal to suchness;
since subsequently attained wisdom does not directly take suchness as its object,
it is not termed "the simultaneous practice of the ultimate and the conventional."
Upon reaching the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), this [wisdom] which was previously difficult to harmonize becomes conjoined and made to correspond;

thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that if one is at the level of the Buddha-fruit (*buddhatva*), this wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) simultaneously takes both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) as its objects.
If it were the case that on the tenth bhūmi one perceives only maturation (vipāka) and is unable to perceive suchness (tathatā),
then the aforementioned fault would not apply; however, this is also not the case.
Among the ten types of equality, it is accepted that [the mind] takes suchness as its object.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, in its fifth fascicle, states that this is attained in the first bhūmi.
Therefore, we know that within the causal stage, one also takes both the conventional and the ultimate as objects.
The former interpretation is superior; alternatively, because the eighth consciousness has not yet been abandoned,
it is called "attaining" when it takes the ālayavijñāna as its object,
for its nature has not yet been separated [from defilement].
Therefore, it is further stated that "etcetera" refers to the syllable *vijñā* (consciousness) and the syllable *ādi* (etcetera),
which both pervade the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) and the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*).
This interpretation is difficult to understand.
Since there is nothing capable of being concealed,
the meaning of "concealment" (āvaraṇa) should be temporarily set aside.
Question: Since the two types of grasping arise together, why are their states and sequences different?
First, [the text] extensively explains the grasping of others.
Treatise:
Because the term "pudgala" (person) is applied only when one reaches the state of being a human and so forth.
Commentary: [As stated above].
From here below is the second section, which further clarifies the preceding stage.
This text consists of two parts, as it only elaborates upon the first two [of the three]. Within the first elaboration, there are two sections.
First, the breadth and narrowness of the two types of grasping are clarified;
subsequently, the identity and difference of their function and essence are clarified.
This is the former.
This now demonstrates that the initial stage necessarily entails the subsequent stages;
because the former is brief,
the stage of the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) must necessarily include the dharma-self (*dharma-ātman*).
This is because the person-self necessarily arises based upon the phenomenon-self;
because the person-self functions as a sovereign controller, an agent, and so forth;
and because the phenomenon-self possesses its own intrinsic nature and superior functions.

This refers to the fact that the self of phenomena (dharma-ātman) is pervasive, whereas the self of persons (pudgala-ātman) is narrow. It is like a person who, being deluded by a tree stump, does not recognize it as a stump and instead grasps at it as a human;
the delusion regarding the stump must precede the arising of the notion of a "person."
Within this analogy, there are varying degrees of depth in the underlying principle.
The shallow analogy is as follows: the person represents the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*), while being deluded by the tree stump represents the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
The profound analogy is that delusion regarding the stump is delusion regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This means that "person" refers to the arising of the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*),
whereas "phenomena" refers to delusion regarding the principle (*tattva*).
Question: Regarding the grasping at phenomena among persons, one might also say that persons are deluded regarding the principle.
Regarding the grasping at phenomena among dharmas, the answer is: not so.
Persons are narrow; dharmas are broad.
Because the Dharma is the fundamental basis, it is difficult to provide a simple analogy.
If one clings to [the stump] as being a person,
one may be made to cling to the stump as being the Dharma-clinging.

Since it has been stated that the delusion regarding a stump arises as [the perception of] a person, the delusion regarding the stump should not be an attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Answer: This is not so.
The one who is deluded does not understand [the true nature of reality].
When one does not ascertain that it is a log, this resembles attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*);

it does not mean that one must first grasp it as a real log before it is considered non-ascertainment. Question: If it is non-ascertainment regarding a log, how does it differ from doubt? Answer: Because that [doubt] consists of indecision.
Because of this certainty, one becomes certain in one's delusion regarding the stump and consequently grasps it as being a person; therefore,
this is an attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Question: How can the two types of grasping arise simultaneously?
Treatise:
The same should apply here regarding the two views of self and phenomena.
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the identity and difference between essence and function. While the self and phenomena are distinct in their functions, [their essences are identical].
The essence of wisdom is one;
thus, for it to arise from the same seeds does not contradict reason.
It is like a single visual consciousness perceiving two objects, such as blue and yellow.
The two modes of activity arise from one another;
however, in this context, consciousness is accepted as having both objects and both modes of activity,
serving as an analogy for the mind that is not shared [with other cognitions].

However, that which is currently maintained is not these two objects, because within a single moment of mind, two modes of apprehension do not arise toward two distinct objects. Question: If that is so, as was previously stated, doubt pertains to principle (*li*), while conviction pertains to phenomena (*shi*). How is this to be understood?
Is it not the case that there are two modes of activity and two objects? Although those [two] are not distinct in their mode of activity, grasping is not so;
this is because it involves investigative searching.
Because they are firmly attached,
objects and modes of activity that are distinct do not arise simultaneously; however,
since this is not the case here, simultaneous arising is admitted.
This is an extensive elaboration of the first person’s adherence to [the existence of] positions (*sthiti*).
Below this, there are three sections that extensively elaborate upon the stage of adherence to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) mentioned previously.
First, there is a general and extensive elaboration on the stage of universal adherence to phenomena alone (*sarva-dharma-mātra-grāha*).
Next, there is further debate regarding the eighth stage and above,
concerning the subsequent interpretation of the meaning of the defiled and non-defiled nature of the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Treatise:
Regarding the statement that "the learners of the two vehicles have already subdued the grasping at a self," the commentary says:
this extensively explains the second stage previously mentioned, the stage of grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Because this interpretation is broad,
and because this dharma-grasping necessarily exists in the initial stage,
there is no need to further explain all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

There is no doubt that this principle holds: for those with personhood-grasping (*pudgala-grāha*) and for those of the two vehicles of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) who are still in training (*śaikṣa*), when the Noble Path arises and they abide in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are present.
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that for a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment,
the entire path of seeing is eliminated;
this is explained according to the single-moment true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*).
Because the contemplation of phenomena as being exclusively [of one nature] contradicts the adherence to [the notion of] a transgression;

if one contemplates with the three minds, then at the time of the first thought-moment, there is only the contemplation of the person. At the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), there arises the knowledge of the emptiness of persons (pudgalanairātmyajñāna) and its fruit.
The fruit consists of the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*),
as well as the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) induced by that emptiness of persons.
This refers to the Bodhisattva of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) who attains enlightenment gradually.
In all stages, when the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena arises,
as well as when the two fruits manifest,
one gives rise exclusively to this consciousness’s grasping at dharmas.
Because these individuals cling to a person, they possess an obstruction to the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of persons. Consequently,
while the noble paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of fixed nature and their meditative absorptions [are attained],
the bodhisattvas— whether of sudden or gradual capacity— have already subdued the clinging to a self regarding both the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons and its resultant state.
Because it can only be severed upon reaching the Vajra-like Mind,
there remains only the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
For both sudden and gradual Bodhisattvas, this is eliminated by the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) on the Path of Seeing, along with its fruit.
This is because they necessarily lack the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
However, among those who give rise to clinging to phenomena alone,
how do the Arhats of the two vehicles of fixed nature and those of this gradual awakening [attain liberation]?
Treatise:
Because the two vehicles, having reached the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), have already severed the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
Commentary: [As stated above.]
This clarifies these two types of persons:
namely, all those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) who are fixed in their nature and have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa),
as well as bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment throughout all their stages.
When the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) and its fruit are not manifest,
whether one abides in a distracted or concentrated mind— whether that mind be contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)— in all cases,
one gives rise solely to the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
Because the grasping at a self has already been severed,
the gradual realization immediately eliminates the entirety of the path of seeing, as well as the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena within the path of cultivation,
and the state in which the fruit is manifest.
Because the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) definitely does not function in this state,
it is not excluded in other states,
as all of them possess grasping at phenomena.
However, if all these refer to those of gradual enlightenment— whether in training (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa)—
or to Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment from the eighth stage (bhūmi) upward,
their great power is similar.
Prior to the seventh stage, the intervals between impure states of mind differ from those of the eighth stage;
because this point follows immediately below [the previous discussion], the treatise addresses it again.
*Treatise:*
"From the eighth stage upward, because they do not contradict one another.
The commentary states:
This refers again to the three stages from the eighth stage upward.
In that stage, the grasping at a self (ātman) no longer functions at all.
There are two ways in which it does not function:
for those who have attained the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) through gradual awakening, it is called "non-functioning" because they have permanently severed it.
For those in training who attain gradual enlightenment,
as well as for Bodhisattvas who attain sudden enlightenment,
these [defilements] are permanently suppressed at this stage and are thus termed "non-functioning."
This refers to the eighth [ground], where the name "equanimity" is abandoned because the objects of cognition no longer function.
In these three grounds, the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena does not manifest.
When one gives rise to the contemplation of persons, one still gives rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
for there is no contradiction between them;
since subtle attachment does not obstruct the arising of coarse contemplation.
If it were not so, one should instead give rise to the contemplation of dharmas,
which is a purely uncontaminated continuity,
uninterrupted by any contaminated mind.
Taking this as proof:
from the eighth stage onward,
if they admit that the sixth mental consciousness can give rise to a contaminated mind, [then...]
Why does the grasping at a self not function in that state?
Because the grasping at a self does not obstruct the outflow-tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*).
Even if the seeds of that grasping at a self have not been permanently severed, they are merely suppressed.
Therefore, it is known that the untainted mind constantly gives rise to the contemplation of persons and phenomena.
What serves as proof for this?
It is as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.
It should be seventy-eight.
This is the fault regarding the two obstacles and three locations.
Treatise.
As stated in the Sūtra: "Up until the cognitive obstructions remain.
The commentary states:
From the eighth stage upward, no afflictions manifest again.
"Only the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) that serves as the basis remains.
This is the text of the Sūtra. [The] Treatise [says]:
This is because the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) should likewise persist therein.
[The author] states:
"All attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onwards..."
This refers to active manifestation (*samudācāra*), not seeds.

This is not the dharma-grasping (*dharmanirmoha*)—both manifest and seed—that exists within the sixth consciousness, for it is taught that [this grasping] can be severed in each and every stage (*bhūmi*).

If one were to argue that this teaching refers to the seventh consciousness’s afflictions, while implying that the seeds of dharma-grasping in other consciousnesses do not have manifest activity; [that would be incorrect].
Regarding the statement that "the active cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) do not exist in this stage," it should likewise be said that the seeds of the afflictions (kleśa-bīja) also persist;
for within the ten stages, the seeds of the seventh consciousness as well as other afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) have not yet been severed.
One should say that in this stage both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions are present.
Why, then, is it said that only the cognitive obstruction remains?
If you say it is because the sixth consciousness can give rise to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), [that is not sufficient].
Regarding the statement "taking the Dharma as one's refuge," to what phenomena does this serve as a basis?
The sixth [consciousness] is not the basis.
The seventh is the basis.
Furthermore, if it is granted that the sixth consciousness gives rise to this defiled mind,
why does it not give rise to the affliction of the grasping at a person?
What dharma acts as an obstacle to prevent [the sixth consciousness] from arising?
It is because one does not perceive at other times that the sixth mental consciousness possesses only the grasping of dharmas (*dharmagrāha*),
for it is never at any time found to possess the grasping of a person (*pudgalagrāha*).
However, regarding the first and second stages mentioned above,
the stage of the equality of nature (*samatā*) and so forth was not mentioned because it is easily understood.

From here below begins the third section, which further explains the meaning of the defilement and non-defilement of the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). Question: Why was it stated above that both the followers of the two vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are entirely possessed of [defilement]?
[The Treatise] says:
"Because the mind associated with the clinging to phenomena does not, until [its cessation], obstruct that wisdom.
The commentary states:
"With respect to the two vehicles and so forth..."
Although these various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are said to be unstained, they are called "stained" in relation to bodhisattvas because they obstruct the wisdom of bodhisattvas.
Because this attachment to phenomena (dharmagrāha) pertains to both types of neutral states,
it is non-obscuring (anivṛta) in relation to the two vehicles,
yet it is also called obscuring-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta) in relation to bodhisattvas.
Because it does not obstruct the two vehicles.
The treatise states:
"This is subsumed under that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*); up to this point, it is called 'universal' (*sarvatraga*)."
The commentary states:
There are four types of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
